HS→NAICS Concordance: Many-to-One Correspondence and Granularity Loss

How aggregation to NAICS level conflates distinct clean-tech value chains

Author

Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab · Johns Hopkins SAIS

Published

April 14, 2026

1 Overview

The NZIPL Green Dictionary maps 372 HS6 product codes across 10 clean technologies to four value-chain stages. Using the official US Census Bureau Schedule B → NAICS concordance (2024), 349 of those HS6 codes resolve to 107 unique NAICS 6-digit industry codes — a 3.3× compression.

Important

The granularity problem: When multiple clean-tech HS6 codes map to the same NAICS code, any firm-level query on that industry (via S&P Capital IQ Pro, ORBIS, Compustat, etc.) cannot distinguish a solar-panel manufacturer from a wind-turbine manufacturer, or a battery-grade lithium miner from a copper miner. The clean-tech signal collapses into a broad industrial bucket.

Level Codes Note
Green Dict HS6 372.0 Product-level granularity
HS6 matched to NAICS 349.0 94% coverage (Census Schedule B)
NAICS 6-digit codes 107.0 Industry-level granularity
Compression ratio 3.3 HS6 per NAICS on average

Of the 108 NAICS codes that cover green dictionary products:

  • 41 are unique — clean, one-to-one HS6→NAICS; firm queries are precise.
  • 7 are high-severity (9+ HS6 each) — these aggregate dozens of distinct clean-tech products, spanning multiple technologies, into a single industry bucket.

Why these 23 codes are unmatched

Category 1 — HS 2017/2022 revision gap (manual mapping required)

The Census Schedule B concordance is anchored to the HS 2022 revision (current as of 2024). Some green-dictionary codes were defined for earlier HS revisions (HS2017, HS2012) and have since been split, merged, or renumbered. Nuclear and magnet codes are most affected: for example, 810990 (Zirconium and articles thereof — a key nuclear fuel-cycle material) existed through HS17 but was subdivided in HS22, and the old heading does not appear in the Census export file. Similarly, several rare-earth and magnet codes that were valid HS12/HS17 entries are absent from the HS22-based Schedule B.

These codes must be mapped manually by inspecting the WCO HS2017→HS2022 correlation table and assigning the successor NAICS code from the new heading. Until that is done, firms dealing in these specific products will be missed by NAICS-based queries.

Category 2 — Import-only Schedule B positions (not in export concordance)

The Census expconcord24.xlsx is an export concordance (Schedule B commodity codes). A small number of HS6 positions — primarily certain process-equipment headings — appear only in US import classifications (HTS, Harmonised Tariff Schedule) and have no Schedule B export equivalent. These products are imported rather than domestically manufactured at a classifiable Schedule B level, so no NAICS production code is assigned.

Category 3 — Agricultural / biofuel feedstock codes

Several biofuel feedstock codes (e.g., sugarcane, palm oil, oilseeds) are classified under agricultural chapters (HS 10–15) which the Census Schedule B covers only partially for export purposes. The Census concordance prioritises manufactured goods; primary agricultural commodities used as industrial inputs are underrepresented.

Implication for S&P Capital IQ Pro matching

Firm-level queries using NAICS will structurally miss any company whose primary product is one of these 23 HS6 codes until manual mappings are added. The gap is concentrated in Nuclear (specialty metals and reactor materials) and Magnets (rare-earth precursors) — precisely the technologies where precise firm identification matters most for industrial-policy analysis.

8 Implications for firm-level matching

8.1 False positives

A query on NAICS 325180 (Other Basic Inorganic Chemical Manufacturing) returns the entire inorganic chemicals industry. The vast majority of those firms produce acids, pigments, and industrial gases with no clean-tech relevance. The 37 green-dict HS codes mapped here are a small fraction of what that NAICS industry actually produces.

8.2 Cross-tech contamination

NAICS 212290 (Other Metal Ore Mining) covers all 10 clean technologies. Lithium miners, cobalt miners, rare-earth miners, and uranium miners are all in the same bucket. Any country-level analysis of “other metal ore mining” will conflate these entirely different supply chains.

8.3 Recommended approach

R1 — HS6 as primary key where possible

For databases with HS-level trade identifiers alongside firm records (US Census LFTTD, Indian customs microdata), match directly at HS6. This avoids NAICS aggregation entirely and preserves full product-level granularity.

R2 — Apply green-dict HS filter as a secondary screen

When a firm-level database only exposes NAICS codes, retrieve all firms in the NAICS bucket and then cross-reference against the green dictionary HS codes via the firm’s import/export activity (if available). This converts a broad industry sweep into a targeted clean-tech filter.

R3 — Flag high-severity NAICS codes in any firm-count output

NAICS 325180, 212290, 333517 each cover 8–10 clean technologies. Any firm count or market-share estimate derived from these codes alone should be labelled as an upper-bound estimate, not a clean-tech-specific figure.

R4 — The 41 unique-mapping NAICS codes are analysis-ready

41 NAICS codes have exactly one green-dict HS6 mapped to them. These are safe to use directly in firm queries with high precision: 212220, 212319, 212322, 311225, 325130, 325193, 325311, 325510, 326220, 326299, 327120, 327215, 327310, 327410, 327991, 331314, 332215, 332510, 332618, 332722, 333132, 333243, 333413, 333612, 333613, 333924, 333996, 334412, 334417, 334510, 334511, 334513, 334519, 335220, 335931, 335932, 336330, 336340, 339991, 339999, 910000.
